title: ARRIRAW vs ProRes: When to Shoot Each Format on Set
summary: Decide when to shoot ARRIRAW or ProRes on ARRI jobs by weighing storage, grade latitude, dailies speed, VFX needs, compatibility, and delivery risk clearly.
body_markdown:
Most crews settle this argument on image quality alone. Image quality is the smallest part of it. The format also sets how many magazines the camera department carries, how long the DIT stays on the cart after wrap, and how soon production knows that yesterday's work is safe. A format the pipeline can't carry loses to a lesser format every time.


Decision factor ARRIRAW tends to fit when ProRes tends to fit when


Storage and offload You have the media, the verified backup capacity, and the hours for large files The day depends on smaller files, faster copies, and limited travel storage


Grade flexibility Exposure, white balance, or the final look may still change significantly in post The look is controlled on set and the grade is expected to be moderate


VFX and plates The work involves keying, CG integration, or LED wall plates VFX is limited, the footage is clean, and ProRes 4444 XQ or 4444 covers the shot work


Editorial speed Editorial can wait for a heavier dailies or proxy process Editorial needs fast access, direct ProRes handling, or lightweight remote review files


Pipeline risk Post has tested the exact camera, color pipeline, and conform path The team benefits from broad NLE, finishing, and review compatibility


Archive and future use Remasters, future HDR trims, or VFX revisions are likely Deliverables are immediate and well-defined, with no need for camera-negative flexibility


The short rule on set: shoot ARRIRAW when the image still has decisions left in it. Heavy VFX, uncertain exposure, an unfinished look. Shoot ProRes when the look is settled and the job needs throughput more than it needs raw sensor access.


## What ARRIRAW and ProRes actually are


ARRIRAW is ARRI's raw camera negative. ARRI describes it as uncompressed, unencrypted sensor data that preserves the camera's natural color response and exposure latitude. ALEV3 cameras record[12-bit log ARRIRAW data](https://www.arri.com/en/learn-help/learn-help-camera-system/pre-postproduction/file-formats-data-handling/arriraw-faq) , and ALEXA 35 records 13-bit log ARRIRAW data. Either way, post still has to debayer it and process it into a viewable RGB image.


That processing step is the point. ARRIRAW leaves the decisions open. The post team can revisit the debayer, the white balance interpretation, and the exposure handling later, inside a controlled finishing environment. Like film negative, it exists to preserve the source rather than to be the fastest file to work with.


ProRes from an ARRI camera is a processed recording. The camera debayers the sensor data and encodes it into an Apple ProRes codec, commonly in LogC or LogC4 depending on camera generation and settings. The quality is still very high, especially in ProRes 4444 XQ and ProRes 4444. It is no longer raw sensor data.


ARRIRAW stays closer to the sensor data, while ProRes is processed in camera into a more editing-friendly file. That distinction counts for more than the wrapper does. Modern ARRI cameras may record both MXF/ARRIRAW and MXF/ProRes, while older workflows may involve QuickTime-wrapped ProRes. ARRI moved newer[ProRes recording into MXF](https://www.arri.com/en/learn-help/learn-help-camera-system/pre-postproduction/file-formats-data-handling/prores) because MXF is an open standard and gives better access to metadata. MXF/ProRes is still ProRes.


ProRes and ProRes RAW are separate things.[ProRes RAW is Apple's raw codec family](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102124) , supported in specific products and workflows. Internal ARRI ProRes recording, as commonly discussed on ALEXA workflows, is conventional ProRes. If someone says “we're shooting ProRes RAW on ARRI,” confirm the exact camera, recorder, and codec, then check the finishing software. That is a different workflow conversation.


## Storage is the real deciding factor


ARRIRAW produces much larger camera originals than ProRes. The exact number depends on the camera, the sensor mode, and the recording option. Resolution and frame rate move it further. The operational pattern holds regardless: ARRIRAW burns through media faster, takes longer to offload, and needs more shuttle storage. It also enlarges everything downstream. Backup drives, nearline storage, and LTO all grow. So do cloud transfer times and finishing storage.


ARRIRAW usually creates a much larger media footprint than ProRes. ProRes is compressed and designed for high-performance post workflows. Apple describes the ProRes family as built for[real-time, multistream editing performance](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/31914/9e205c6174d911712c76cf3258e0d95a/2022-04-apple-prores-white-paper-data.pdf) with reduced storage rates. ProRes is intraframe and variable bit rate, so every frame is self-contained and simpler for edit systems to decode than many long-GOP codecs. That is a large part of why it took over editorial and finishing.


For a production team, the format decision touches several practical resources:


- Camera media count and reload rhythm
- Checksum verification time
- Number and size of backup drives
- Dailies render time
- Storage required for conform and grade


Plenty of productions shoot ARRIRAW every day. They budget it as a workflow first and pick the camera setting second. If the DIT cart, the storage, and the post facility are all sized for ProRes, switching to ARRIRAW can break the day even though the camera records it fine.


On ALEXA 35 and newer ARRI workflows, camera generation brings extra format options and efficiencies. Those include ARRIRAW-related footprint reduction and newer ARRI formats like ARRICORE. ARRICORE isn't ARRIRAW and isn't ProRes, but it exists because productions increasingly want high image quality with a smaller footprint. If the show is on a camera that supports those choices, put them in the workflow test.


## Where the grade starts to show the difference


In a normal grade with well-exposed footage, good lighting, and a clear show LUT, ProRes looks excellent. ARRI ProRes has finished high-end work for years because the camera's color science and LogC encoding hold up extremely well. If the DP is exposing carefully and the finishing target is SDR or a controlled HDR pass without aggressive rescue work, ProRes 4444 XQ or ProRes 4444 is more than enough.


The differences show up when the grade asks the image to stretch.


Aggressive grading can reveal where one recording format holds detail better than another. ARRIRAW gives the colorist more room in situations like these:


- Major white balance changes after the shoot
- Underexposed scenes that need shadow recovery
- Mixed lighting where color separation matters
- Heavy HDR highlight shaping
- Debayer choices for final resolution and texture


ProRes still grades beautifully, but it arrives already processed into a video image. The 422 variants also carry less chroma information than the 4444 variants. In straightforward editorial and finishing that rarely shows. It shows in hard keys, deep saturation, and heavy secondary corrections.


This is where the ProRes flavor decides the outcome. ProRes 422 Proxy belongs in editorial as a proxy and nowhere near a finishing master. ProRes 422 HQ is robust for many productions, especially broadcast, branded, and fast-turnaround work. ProRes 4444 and 4444 XQ are the right call when ProRes is the acquisition master and the project still expects a serious grade, compositing, or premium delivery.


ProRes can grade. The real question is how much you expect to change the image later, and what it costs you if you can't.


## Dailies and editorial throughput


Dailies are where the format choice becomes visible to the whole production. ARRI describes dailies as[color corrected and properly framed versions](https://www.arri.com/en/learn-help/learn-help-camera-system/pre-postproduction/editorial-workflow) of the clips shot each day, created after multiple backups of the original camera negative. They are the bridge from set to post, and they let editorial start while the show is still shooting.


ARRIRAW dailies require debayering and color processing. That means more compute, more time, and more attention to color management. The dailies team has to get several things right at once:


- The correct camera color pipeline and look files
- CDL and LUT decisions
- Framing
- Audio sync and timecode
- Naming and metadata handling


None of that is unusual. It is all real work, and it takes real hours.


With ProRes, the path is faster. The camera has already produced a high-quality RGB or YCbCr image in a post-friendly codec. Depending on the editorial system and storage, editorial can cut ProRes directly, or your team can transcode it into lighter editorial proxies. This is the origin of ARRI's “direct-to-edit” history with ALEXA and ProRes. It doesn't mean every show should edit original camera files. It does mean the source format is friendlier to fast editorial access.


A production that needs same-day edits, fast documentary turnaround, or remote editorial upload will benefit from ProRes. ARRIRAW still works there, but only if the dailies system is built for it.


Editorial planning comes down to a handful of questions:


- Will editorial cut camera originals, mezzanine files, or proxies?
- Will your team make dailies on set, near set, or at a lab?
- Is the upload path sized for OCN, proxies, or both?
- Will the dailies software, the NLE, or both handle sound sync?
- Is the show LUT/look metadata traveling consistently into editorial?
- Will the conform return to ARRIRAW, ProRes masters, or rendered graded media?


Those answers shape the format choice more than theory does. A short commercial with a finishing house ready for ARRIRAW is the easier job. A documentary traveling with a tiny crew and weak internet is the harder one, even though it shoots far more footage.


## VFX pulls, plates, and metadata


For VFX-heavy work, shoot ARRIRAW. Green screen, set extensions, CG integration, and heavy plate manipulation all benefit from maximum source data. ARRIRAW gives the VFX and DI teams more control over debayering, color transforms, and exposure interpretation, and it leaves noise handling open.


There is one real exception. VFX teams deliver finished shots from ProRes 4444 and 4444 XQ every day, when the work is limited and the photography is clean. That exception stops applying somewhere around hundreds of shots, complicated keys, or underexposed plates. LED wall interaction and extensive roto and comp end it as well.


Metadata carries weight here too. ARRI notes that modern ALEXA cameras store per-frame and per-shot metadata in recorded formats such as MXF/ARRIRAW and MXF/ProRes. The camera can also capture active look files as metadata. That helps. It is not a replacement for a real VFX data package.


Recorded media carries technical metadata that matters for post, VFX, and conform. VFX teams need much more than the codec:


- Camera reports and clip metadata
- Lens metadata when available
- Frame lines and extraction notes
- Lens grids
- HDRI and witness camera material
- Color pipeline notes
- Show LUTs, CDLs, and viewing transforms
- Plate handles and retime information
- Any in-camera texture, sharpening, or noise reduction settings


ARRIRAW protects the image. It does nothing to protect the handoff. ProRes with a complete data package will beat ARRIRAW with a messy one, so build the package before you argue about the codec.


## Compatibility means more than opening the file


ProRes has the broadest practical compatibility of any camera master format. The four major NLEs all read it: Final Cut Pro, Premiere Pro, Media Composer, Resolve. So do most finishing and review systems, along with transcoders and many asset platforms. Final Cut Pro supports every ProRes version. That is one reason ProRes stays a safe choice for fast-moving productions.


ARRIRAW support is also common in professional post, but it is more version-sensitive. You need support for the exact camera generation, wrapper, and resolution, and for that camera's color science and metadata. ALEXA 35 introduced[LogC4 and the REVEAL color pipeline](https://www.arri.com/resource/blob/277396/5a14858a5279638c1e0756d67e94a7d7/2022-05-alexa-35-workflow-post-guide-launch-data.pdf) , so old assumptions from LogC3 workflows may not hold. A pipeline that hasn't been updated can import ARRIRAW and still display it incorrectly, lose metadata behavior, or demand extra conversion steps.


The same applies to MXF. ARRI's newer cameras use MXF for both ARRIRAW and ProRes, and ARRI states that the camera stores metadata in the file header. That is good for professional workflows, but tools built around QuickTime ProRes habits need testing. “It supports ProRes” isn't specific enough. The useful sentence names the camera's MXF/ProRes, the resolution and frame rate, and the LogC version, and it confirms the metadata survives the trip.


The practical compatibility test should include the actual route the footage will take:


- Offload and checksum tool
- Dailies software
- Sound sync path
- Editorial NLE
- Assistant editor relink workflow
- VFX pull tool
- Color grading system
- Archive and restore process
- Any remote review or cloud proxy workflow


[Run a short camera test](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MU6lI4zHXB4) down that entire path before the show starts. One application opening the file proves nothing. Most format problems appear at the handoffs: dailies to editorial, conform to grade, archive to restore.


## Delivery doesn't automatically require ARRIRAW


Delivery specs influence acquisition without always dictating it. A streamer, studio, or distributor may specify approved cameras, minimum raster, or HDR and archival deliverables. Broadcasters do the same. If the spec requires raw acquisition, the decision has been made for you. If it allows ProRes, you still have to judge whether ProRes carries the creative and post plan.


For theatrical finishing, HDR mastering, and premium episodic, ARRIRAW is attractive because the negative remains maximally reprocessable. That is what long-term library value means in practice. Future remasters, alternate trims, and new HDR passes all pull from the raw source, and so do late VFX revisions.


For corporate, documentary, and branded work, ProRes makes more sense. The same goes for social, event, and fast-turnaround broadcast jobs. The audience will never see the difference when the lighting, exposure, and lensing are good and the color management is clean. They will notice a missed deadline, a delayed edit, or a production that ran out of storage at lunch.


Delivery is the final output. Acquisition is the bet you place on how safely the production gets there.


## Common ways the choice goes wrong


Most ARRIRAW versus ProRes problems come from choosing a format the workflow can't support. Almost none come from choosing the theoretically wrong format.


The common failure patterns are predictable:


- The team selects ARRIRAW, but the production doesn't add enough recording media.
- The team estimates offload time from file copy speed instead of checksum-verified backup time.
- Editorial assumes direct playback of OCN on hardware that can't handle it.
- The team chooses ProRes 422 for a VFX-heavy job that really needed 4444 XQ or ARRIRAW.
- ALEXA 35 LogC4 material enters a LogC3-based pipeline.


ARRI's data handling guidance is direct about one thing: avoid simple file copy methods for original camera data. Use[checksum-verified backups](https://www.arri.com/en/learn-help/learn-help-camera-system/pre-postproduction/data-transfer) . That holds whether the camera is recording ARRIRAW or ProRes. Smaller ProRes files move faster. They are no less important.


## A decision model for set


In prep, start with the hardest part of the job instead of the average shot. One greenscreen day, one night exterior, or one sequence with no locked look can justify ARRIRAW even if the rest of the show would survive on ProRes. The reverse holds too. A single prestige scene doesn't justify ARRIRAW across a six-week documentary when the storage, the travel, and the editorial schedule make it unmanageable.


ARRIRAW is the better call when the project has these conditions:


- High-end narrative, commercial, or premium episodic finishing
- Heavy VFX, keying, cleanup, or CG integration
- Aggressive HDR grade or uncertain final look
- Significant reframing, extraction, or stabilization
- Enough media, storage, backup, and dailies capacity


ProRes is the better call when the project has these conditions:


- Fast editorial turnaround
- Limited storage or travel footprint
- Remote collaboration with large upload constraints
- Controlled lighting and exposure
- Minimal VFX


For many jobs the answer is mixed. Shoot ARRIRAW for VFX plates, night work, and any scene whose look is still unsettled. Shoot ProRes 4444 XQ, 4444, or 422 HQ for everything else, depending on the finishing target. Mixed-format shows need clear camera reports and tight editorial communication, and they save enormous amounts of storage without giving up raw where it counts.


Camera, post, and production should make this call together, with editorial in the room. The DP owns the image intent. The assistant editor, the post supervisor, and the DIT know whether the chosen format can move through the pipeline without breaking schedule or budget. So does the colorist.


So make it concrete in prep. Take the hardest day on the schedule. Price its ARRIRAW media, its offload hours, and its dailies compute. See whether that number survives contact with the budget. If it does, shoot ARRIRAW on that day and ProRes on the rest. If it doesn't, shoot ProRes 4444 and light for it.


## FAQ


No. ARRIRAW keeps the image as raw camera data, which preserves the most flexibility. It also increases storage, offload time, and dailies processing, and it complicates post. ProRes is the better choice when the look is controlled and the grade isn't expected to be extreme. It is also the better choice when editorial needs fast access or the production can't support a raw workflow.


For serious finishing, use ProRes 4444 XQ or ProRes 4444. Both preserve more color information than the 422 variants. ProRes 422 HQ is still appropriate for many broadcast, documentary, and fast-turnaround jobs. Treat ProRes 422 Proxy as an editorial proxy format only, never as a high-quality acquisition master.


ARRIRAW has to be debayered and processed into a viewable image before editorial dailies exist. That costs compute time. It also demands correct color management, look files, and metadata handling, plus framing and audio sync. ProRes arrives already processed in camera into a post-friendly video file, so it can move into dailies and editorial faster.


Yes, when the footage is clean, well exposed, and recorded in a high-quality ProRes format such as 4444 or 4444 XQ. ARRIRAW is still preferred for heavy keying, compositing, and underexposed plates. The same goes for CG integration, beauty work, and LED wall work, and for any shot that needs substantial manipulation. ARRIRAW gives VFX and DI teams more control over debayering, color, and exposure interpretation, and it leaves noise handling open.


Test the real path from camera to delivery. That means verified offload and backup, then dailies and sound sync. Then editorial import, relink, and VFX pulls. Then conform, grade, review, archive, and restore. Use the exact camera model, recording format, and resolution planned for production, with the same wrapper, frame rate, color science, LUTs, and metadata workflow. A file opening in one application proves nothing about the rest of the pipeline.


Mixed-format shows need consistent clip naming, camera reports, and color pipeline notes. They also need metadata that says which scenes are raw, which are ProRes, and which files are editorial proxies rather than finishing masters. Aspect tracks those attributes in searchable project-level fields, so assistants and post supervisors can filter by format, LUT status, or VFX status, and by delivery stage, using custom metadata.
